question:
Patient note:
A 28-year-old woman with no recorded medical history and taking only a combined oral contraceptive pill was transferred by rural ground EMS after being discovered at 13:40 lying prone on a rocky riverbank beneath a collapsed bouldering wall; companions stated she had fallen roughly four meters, struck the left parietal region on limestone, and was briefly motionless before emitting incoherent phrases such as “where are my shoes” and “the water’s upside-down,” then lapsed into silence with her eyes shut. Paramedics arrived nine minutes after the call, placed a rigid collar, rolled her onto a scoop stretcher with head blocks, established a single 18-gauge IV in the right antecubital vein but left it saline-locked, checked a capillary glucose of 112 mg/dL, and delivered 10 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask; no crystalloid bolus, analgesic, sedative, paralytic, dextrose, naloxone, anticonvulsant, or vasoactive medication was administered en route during the fifteen-minute transport so the neurologic examination would remain unaltered. She arrived in our resuscitation bay at 14:09 still secured to the scoop, clothing damp from river spray and lightly dusted with chalk, a 3-cm ragged scalp laceration oozing along the superior margin of the left pinna. Pre-intervention vital signs recorded simultaneously with the first in-hospital neurologic survey are blood pressure 142/88 mm Hg in the right brachial artery, heart rate 102 beats/min in regular sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with shallow thoracoabdominal excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % on the same mask, and tympanic temperature 37.1 °C. Airway inspection reveals intact dentition, minimal dried blood on the hard palate, no pooled secretions, and a Yankauer sweep to the oropharynx prompts a brisk cough and gag. During an initial 30-second period of quiet observation she lies motionless, eyelids fully closed without fluttering and no spontaneous limb activity. When her given name is called at conversational and then shouted volume adjacent to either ear, there is no lid separation, no verbal reply, and no extremity movement. A firm supra-orbital ridge pressure applied for five seconds, however, causes both eyelids to spring open half-way; pupils 3 mm bilaterally constrict briskly to direct light, gaze drifts past the examiner, and the lids fall shut within two seconds once the stimulus stops. Immediately after eye opening she utters slurred but intelligible phrases—“I’m late for the train,” “don’t let the cats out”—that do not correspond to questions about her identity or location, and she becomes intermittently querulous, asking “why is it snowing?” despite being indoors. When asked her name she provides a childhood nickname, gives the month as “Octember,” and cannot recall the accident, demonstrating obvious disorientation though sentence structure remains intact. Upper extremities at rest display normal bulk and baseline tone. Nail-bed compression of the right index finger elicits rapid adduction of both shoulders, elbows flex to approximately 90 degrees with forearm pronation, and wrists curl inward; lower limbs simultaneously extend slightly at the knees with plantar flexion. The posture persists two seconds beyond removal of the stimulus before the limbs relax. A sternal rub reproduces an identical flexor pattern without any purposeful reach toward the examiner’s hand. No spontaneous purposeful movement is observed between stimuli, and she fails to follow simple commands such as “show two fingers” or “stick out your tongue.” Deep tendon reflexes are 3 + at biceps and patellae, 2 + at Achilles; there is no clonus and plantar responses are mute. Cranial nerve assessment confirms symmetric corneal reflexes, midline tongue when the jaw is passively opened, and facial grimace present with nail-bed pain. Cardiovascular exam reveals a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs; distal pulses are 2 +, capillary refill under two seconds. Lungs are clear to auscultation with equal breath sounds and resonant percussion; no paradoxical chest wall motion is noted. Abdomen is flat, soft, nontender, with active bowel sounds; pelvis is stable. Log-roll inspection shows mild ecchymosis over the left scapular ridge but no step-off; spine palpation is midline and non-tender. Extremities demonstrate no deformity, and distal neurovascular status is intact. Skin is warm and well perfused; aside from the scalp laceration there are superficial abrasions over the right forearm and left knee. Point-of-care venous blood gas on current oxygen flow reveals pH 7.37, pCO₂ 39 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear lung fields and normal mediastinal silhouette; pelvic X-ray is unremarkable. Blood for complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, coagulation studies, serum ethanol, and type-and-screen has been drawn but not yet resulted. No pharmacologic agents or intravenous fluids other than the prehospital saline lock have been given in the department, ensuring that the ocular, verbal, and motor behaviors detailed above represent her untreated neurologic baseline. Neurosurgery and trauma surgery have been paged; urgent non-contrast CT of the head, maxillofacial CT, and cervical spine CT are being arranged, and nursing staff have instituted fifteen-minute neurologic checks while airway equipment for possible rapid-sequence intubation stands ready should her mental status deteriorate.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses on the untreated admission examination.
Eye: Her eyes remain closed to voice and open only to supraorbital pressure → E2.
Verbal: She answers questions about her name and the month but is disoriented. Her best response is confused conversation, not just unrelated words → V4.
Motor: Pain elicits stereotyped elbow flexion, forearm pronation, and wrist flexion, without withdrawal or localization. This is abnormal flexion → M3.
Sum: 2 + 4 + 3 = 9.
Final answer: 9
